findings.claim: The Crofts are described as "an old country family - landed people"
findings.truth: The line is "an old county family - landed people", and Birling says it of Lady Croft (Gerald's mother), not of the Crofts as a family.
findings.evidence: Act 1: "Don't blame her. She comes from an old county family - landed people and so forth." (archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley')

findings.claim: Flashcard 14 answer: "The Crofts - Gerald's 'old country family - landed people.'"
findings.truth: Same error: "old county family", said of Lady Croft.
findings.evidence: As F1.

findings.claim: The play "premiered at the Kamerny Theatre in Moscow on 1 October 1945"
findings.truth: The Soviet premiere was in May 1945 (Moscow Kamerny Theatre and Leningrad Comedy Theatre). 1 October is the London date (New Theatre, 1946).
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Inspector_Calls - "first performed in the Soviet Union in May 1945"

findings.claim: Flashcard 4 answer: "The Kamerny Theatre in Moscow, on 1 October 1945."
findings.evidence: As F3.

findings.claim: Practice questions 3 and 5 are labelled "4 marks - Quote Analysis"; questions 3, 4 and 5 carry ladders running to 8, 12 and 4 marks. The same pattern repeats in ALL EIGHT lessons (24 questions).
findings.truth: Component 01 Section A has one compulsory question in two 20-mark parts. There is no 4-mark, 8-mark or 12-mark question on this text. Every question relabelled "20 marks" and every malformed ladder rescaled to five equal house bands (17-20 / 13-16 / 9-12 / 5-8 / 1-4).
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md, "Forms of assessment": Section A = 40 marks, one extended response split into (a) comparison with an unseen same-genre extract AND (b) a related question.

findings.claim: "His broadcasts were so politically powerful that the government eventually took them off the air."
findings.truth: Postscripts ended in October 1940. Who ended them is disputed - Priestley blamed the BBC and the Ministry of Information; the "Churchill silenced him" story is contested. The lesson states it as settled fact twice (content and flashcard 9).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia / J.B. Priestley Society; no primary source names "the government".

findings.claim: Key-fact revision tip: "what does the Inspector mean by 'these girls aren't cheap labour - they're people'?"
findings.truth: The line is Sheila's (Act 1). The lesson body attributes it to Sheila, so the tip contradicts the lesson.
findings.evidence: "SHEILA: But these girls aren't cheap labour - they're people." (archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley')

findings.claim: Question 3: "Analyse how Priestley uses the Inspector's line 'these girls aren't cheap labour...'"
findings.truth: Sheila's line, not the Inspector's.
findings.evidence: As F7.

findings.claim: Flashcard 10: "What quotation sums up the Inspector's challenge to Birling's view of workers?"
findings.truth: The quotation given is Sheila's.
findings.evidence: As F7.

findings.claim: "When Sheila says 'these girls aren't cheap labour - they're people,' Birling dismisses her entirely."
findings.truth: Sheila answers the INSPECTOR, who has just said factories look for cheap labour ("Ask your father"). The Inspector replies drily; Birling says nothing to her.
findings.evidence: Act 1 exchange, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Birling is "in the running" for a knighthood; the engagement joins the Birlings and Crofts - "one of the oldest county families".
findings.truth: Neither phrase is in the play. Birling says there is "a fair chance that I might find my way into the next Honours List", and hopes Crofts and Birlings will be "working together - for lower costs and higher prices".
findings.evidence: Act 1, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Flashcard 9 answer: "an impression of 'massiveness - solidity - purposefulness'"
findings.truth: The stage direction reads "an impression of massiveness, solidity and purposefulness".
findings.evidence: Act 1 stage direction, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: The Act 2 closing stage direction is quoted as "Eric enters, looking extremely pale and distressed. They stare at him. He comes in, the door slowly closes behind him. Curtain," and the "slow-closing door" is then analysed as a symbol.
findings.truth: The direction reads: "We hear the front door. They wait, looking towards door. Eric enters, looking extremely pale and distressed. He meets their inquiring stares." There is no closing door.
findings.evidence: End of Act Two, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Exam tip tells students to analyse "the slow-closing door".
findings.truth: The device does not exist; the act ends on the silent stares.
findings.evidence: As F13.

findings.claim: Question 6 mark scheme: "The slow-closing door is symbolic - sealing the family's fate. The silence ('They stare')..."
findings.truth: Same invented direction; "They stare" is not the wording either.
findings.evidence: As F13.

findings.claim: Flashcard 14 answer: "Eric enters 'pale and distressed'; the door slowly closes behind him; curtain."
findings.truth: Same invented direction.
findings.evidence: As F13.

findings.claim: Sheila refuses to leave with "Why should I? It's my turn to ask questions."
findings.truth: Invented. Sheila says "you haven't finished asking questions - have you? ... Then I'm staying"; "Why should you?" is Gerald's reply.
findings.evidence: Act 2 opening, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Mrs Birling "declares that the father should be held 'entirely responsible - he should be dealt with very severely'".
findings.truth: Two separate lines merged into one quotation: "Then he'd be entirely responsible-" and, later, "And he ought to be dealt with very severely-" / "he should be made an example of".
findings.evidence: Act 2, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Gerald says Eva "didn't blame me at all. I must say she didn't."
findings.truth: The line is "She didn't blame me at all. I wish to God she had now."
findings.evidence: Act 2, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: "his family are 'an old country family - landed people'" (also flashcard 15).
findings.truth: As F1: "old county family", said of Lady Croft.
findings.evidence: Act 1, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: "they telephone the infirmary and discover that no girl has died... They call the police and learn there is no Inspector Goole on the force."
findings.truth: Order and agents are wrong. Gerald MET a police sergeant in the street who knew of no Inspector Goole; Birling then telephoned the chief constable, Colonel Roberts, to confirm it; only after that did Gerald ring the infirmary.
findings.evidence: Act 3: "I met a police sergeant I know down the road"; "Ring up the chief constable - Colonel Roberts"; "By ringing up the Infirmary." (archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley')

findings.claim: Flashcard 11: "What two calls does Gerald make...?" - "He phones the infirmary (no death) and the police (no Inspector Goole)."
findings.truth: Gerald makes ONE call (the infirmary); the sergeant was met in person and the chief constable was rung by Birling.
findings.evidence: As F21.

findings.claim: Sheila is quoted as saying "It doesn't make any difference - you still did the things you did." The same invented line appears in lessons 5, 7 and 8, in three flashcards, one knowledge check, one match option and three practice questions.
findings.truth: Her line is "All right. But it doesn't make any real difference, y'know." The "you still did the things you did" half does not exist.
findings.evidence: Act 3, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Eric: "Then - you killed her. She came to you for help and you turned her away."
findings.truth: "Then - you killed her. She came to you to protect me - and you turned her away."
findings.evidence: Act 3, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Mrs Birling deflects onto the Inspector: "I consider you conducted this enquiry in a most peculiar manner."
findings.truth: Invented wording, and placed after the reveal. In Act 2 she says he seems "to be conducting [it] in a rather peculiar and offensive manner"; after he leaves she says "his manner was quite extraordinary; so - so rude - and assertive".
findings.evidence: Acts 2 and 3, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: "She only had herself to blame" (also lesson 5 Q2 mark scheme, lesson 8 content and flashcard 7).
findings.truth: The line is "I think she had only herself to blame."
findings.evidence: Act 2, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: The play ends with the family "staring, dumbfounded" (also lesson 6 content, question 6 and flashcard 15).
findings.truth: The final direction is "As they stare guiltily and dumbfounded, the curtain falls." The dropped word is "guiltily", which carries the meaning.
findings.evidence: End of Act Three, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Gerald suggests "if they don't believe us, they can come and look at her".
findings.truth: Invented. Gerald proposes to settle it "by ringing up the Infirmary. Either there's a dead girl there or there isn't."
findings.evidence: Act 3, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: "his family are 'an old country family - landed people'"
findings.truth: As F1.
findings.evidence: Act 1, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Gerald challenges the photograph technique: "We didn't see the photograph, did we?"
findings.truth: Invented. In Act 1 he asks "Any particular reason why I shouldn't see this girl's photograph, Inspector?"; in Act 3, "How do you know it's the same photograph?"
findings.evidence: archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: "When Birling threatens him - mentioning his friendship with the Chief Constable and his potential knighthood - the Inspector responds: 'Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges.'"
findings.truth: The line answers Birling's "No, for being so offensive about it. I'm a public man-" after Birling demands an apology. The chief constable is mentioned much earlier and not here.
findings.evidence: Act 2, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Chain of events given as "Birling... Sheila... Gerald... Mrs Birling denied her charity, Eric assaulted her."
findings.truth: Chronologically Eric comes before Mrs Birling: Birling (Sept 1910), Sheila (Milwards, early 1911), Gerald (March-Sept 1911), Eric (late 1911, the pregnancy), Mrs Birling (the committee, two weeks before the death). Only the interrogation order puts Mrs Birling first.
findings.evidence: Acts 1-3 timeline, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: Question 1: "Read the extract where the Inspector says 'these girls aren't cheap labour - they're people.'"
findings.truth: Sheila's line.
findings.evidence: As F7.

findings.claim: Flashcard 12: "Quote Birling's gendered dismissal of striking workers." - "He treats them as 'cheap labour' rather than people."
findings.truth: Birling never says "cheap labour" (the Inspector uses it, Sheila rejects it), the answer supplies no quotation although the question asks for one, and nothing in it is gendered. Rewritten as a Sheila quotation card.
findings.evidence: Act 1, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.claim: "the landed aristocracy (Gerald's family, 'an old country family - landed people')" (also flashcard 11).
findings.truth: As F1.
findings.evidence: Act 1, archive.org 'an-inspector-calls-full-text' (UK acting text) + Dramatists Play Service text 'an-inspector-calls-by-j.-b.-priestley'

findings.truth: The claim itself is correct for this text. The house validator only blocks "Component 1" (single digit), so "Component 01" passes, but it is a spec code in spirit. Left alone here - worth a fleet-wide ruling.

findings.truth: Both are legal; the unit now shows both names. A fleet-wide normalisation to the house names would tidy it. Not edited here.

summary: All eight lessons carry at least one finding. The big ones are an invented Sheila line ("you still did the things you did") propagated across four lessons, an invented Act 2 closing stage direction (a slow-closing door), Sheila's "cheap labour" line handed to the Inspector, a reversed account of the Act 3 phone calls, and "old country family" for "old county family". Every lesson also carried invented 4/8/12-mark question labels and ladders for a board whose only modern-drama questions are worth 20 marks.
